title: Formed to bear it
hook: whatever happens, you're either made to bear it or not; if not, it will end (Meditations 10.3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: will you ever be good? Your line was simple and whole. What true thing did you let show? Day six hundred fourteen.

A long night in a hospital waiting room. A hard season at work. A grief that isn't going anywhere fast. Someone tells you, you're stronger than you think. Sometimes that helps. Sometimes it feels like being handed a heavier box. Marcus has his own version of that sentence in book ten, but his is stranger, and in an odd way more honest, because it has two halves. Today: formed to bear it.
screen: `A LONG NIGHT IN A WAITING ROOM.` → `STRONGER THAN YOU THINK?` → `FORMED TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the fork. Everything that happens, Marcus writes, happens either in a way you're formed by nature to bear, or in a way you're not. Second, the first half. If it's the kind you're formed to bear, don't complain. Bear it, as you were made to. Third, the second half. If it's the kind you're not formed to bear, don't complain either, because it will come to an end, once it has used you up. That's blunt, and it's meant to be honest. For Marcus, nothing truly unbearable goes on forever; it has an end built into it. Fourth, the twist. Then he adds the sentence that carries the most weight: remember that you're formed to bear everything that your own judgment can make bearable, by thinking of it as in your interest, or as your duty. In other words, a great deal of what feels impossible is made heavier by the story we tell about it. Change the story, and the weight can change. That isn't a promise for every pain. Some pain is in the body, some is grief, and no story removes it. Nothing in this passage says you have to carry anything alone, either; asking for help is also a way of bearing. But Marcus's question is worth keeping: which part of this weight is the thing itself, and which part is what I've told myself about it?
screen: `EITHER YOU CAN BEAR IT, OR NOT.` · `IF YOU CAN, BEAR IT.` · `IF NOT, IT WILL END.` · `JUDGMENT MAKES MUCH BEARABLE.` · then, large: `MADE TO BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been carrying: a moderate weight, not the heaviest. Look at it in two parts. First, the thing itself: what's actually happening. Second, the story on top of it: it's not fair, it'll never change, I can't. Breathe, and see whether one piece of the story could be set down. Then ask: can I bear this, today? If yes, bear it. If not, remember it won't last forever, and that you can ask for help. The bell holds the time.
Formed to bear it. Marcus's fork: either you're made to bear this, so bear it, or you're not, and then it will end. And judgment can make much of it bearable. Today's word.
Your line: made to bear it. When something feels too heavy today, ask which part is the thing and which part is the story, and say your line. Day six hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often separate a hardship into the event itself and the judgments added to it, and work on the judgments, while still seeking practical and medical help where it's needed.

fork.setup: something hard has happened. you're Marcus. what does book ten tell you to ask first?
options: am I formed to bear this, and how much is my judgment adding?
how can I avoid feeling anything?
fork.reveal: everything is either bearable by nature or not, he writes; and you're formed to bear whatever your judgment can make bearable.

original.note: Greek: to bear, to carry, the verb used for carrying a load.

trapdoor: what it means: either you can bear it, so bear it; or you can't, and it will end; and much of the weight is what you tell yourself.
what a scholar hears: this is a dilemma argument, one of Marcus's favorite forms: either way, complaint has no place.

notes: 10.3 paraphrased (Long: 'Everything which happens either happens in such wise as thou art formed by nature to bear it, or as thou art not formed by nature to bear it... if not, do not complain, for it will perish after it has consumed thee. But remember that thou art formed by nature to bear everything, with respect to which it depends on thine own opinion to make it endurable and tolerable, by thinking that it is either thy interest or thy duty to do this.'). Confirm.

Sensitive: 'it will perish after it has consumed thee' could be heard by a listener in crisis as being about their own death. The script renders it gently ('it will come to an end, once it has used you up') and adds that asking for help is a way of bearing. A Keeper should check the tone.
